summary: Same 1D red-fire idea on both sides — hot source at pixel 0, embers streaming right, black past the flame tip — but the port's fire settles about half as bright, roughly a third shorter, markedly redder (thin yellow core vs the original's wide one), spikier in texture, and ~1.7x faster at the default 20 fps.
observations: Neither side exposes any settable control (probe: 'no settable controls' on orig and port) — control surfaces match, so there is nothing to dial.

Structure matches in family: on the 60 px strip both draw a saturated hot source at pixel 0 with heat/embers advecting rightward and decaying to black, palette black -> deep red -> orange -> yellow -> white-hot flecks at the base. Waterfalls (baseline, scan20, seed7) read as the same pattern idea on both sides.

Brightness, settled state: over 60 s at 20 fps the original ramps from mean brightness ~56 (first 5 s) to a steady ~100-120 and holds there (avg 95.6, max 133); the port is flat at ~50-60 the whole time (avg 53.5, max 99, brightnessTrend 'steady'). Same gap at seed 7 (orig 98 / port 56) and seed 1234 (orig 99 / port 58) over 40 s.

Because the original's warm-up is frame-COUNT driven, the two sides look nearly identical over a short window and diverge later: the 6 s baseline is orig mean 55 vs port 54, while 60 s at 20 fps is 96 vs 53. A 6-second judgement on this pair would have called it a match.

Flame length: in the original's hot regime (skip 30, 10 s, 20 fps) the mean-luminance half-max sits at pixel 31 on the original and pixel 22 on the port; mean luminance at pixel 40 is 59 (orig) vs 20 (port), at pixel 50 it is 30 (orig) vs 5 (port). The original keeps the far end of the strip faintly lit (mean R 27 at px 59); the port is effectively black past ~px 52.

Colour distribution: the original is much yellower. Over 60 s at 20 fps meanG is 86.5 (orig) vs 37.5 (port) and meanB is 14.6 vs 3.1, while meanR is 186 vs 120. In the hot regime the yellow core (mean G > 100) spans pixels 0-26 on the original but only 0-8 on the port. The gap is present from the start, not only after warm-up: over t=2-12 s, mean G at pixel 10 is 143 (orig) vs 87 (port) and at pixel 20 is 78 vs 25.
White-hot flecks: mean B at the base peaks around 109-142 (px 0-3) on the original versus 38-52 on the port in the same hot window — the original's fire root reads white/near-white far more often.

Texture: the original's waterfall streaks are broad, smooth, overlapping slabs; the port's are thinner, higher-frequency individual ember trails with more black between them (visible at every window: baseline, scan20, seed7, hot-regime).

Motion direction and character agree (both advect strictly rightward from px 0, no bounce, no reversal), but speed differs at the default rate. Normalised template-matching of a fixed 26 px window between frames 0.1 s apart gives: original 19.9 / 33.1 / 67.3 px/s at 10 / 20 / 40 fps, port 57.3 / 55.5 / 57.6 px/s at the same rates. The original is FRAME-STEPPED at ~1.7-2 px/frame; the port is time-based and fps-invariant. At the default 20 fps the port is ~1.7x too fast; the two would coincide near 34 fps.

Caution for a fixer: the `motion` stat is useless for this diagnosis here — it reads 12 / 12 / 12 for the original and 16 / 12 / 8 for the port across 10 / 20 / 40 fps, i.e. exactly inverted from the truth. Only position tracking settles it.

The original freezes solid for long stretches on our engine (zero motion 36.2-60.0 s in the 5 fps survey, 54.5-60.0 s at 20 fps; the 120 s survey shows the freezes are ~33 s long and alternate with active stretches). This is the known engine clock artefact seen on the sibling fire-blue, not a port defect, and is not scored. The port never freezes (1 zero-motion frame out of 1200, the unavoidable first frame).
Both sides are alive with no compile or runtime errors, both ignore sensors (wantsSensors false), and both start black and light up within the first second.
feedback: Raise the port's overall heat. In its settled state the original sits at mean brightness ~100-120 over the whole strip while the port sits at ~53-58 — roughly a factor of two. Caveat before chasing an exact number: the original's climb to that level is frame-count driven on our engine (60 s at 5 fps leaves it at mean 60, the same 60 s at 20 fps reaches 96), so target the hot settled look rather than a literal multiplier.

Extend the flame. Mean-luminance half-max should land near pixel 31 of 60, not pixel 22, and the far third of the strip should stay faintly ember-lit (mean R ~27 at pixel 59) instead of going fully black past ~pixel 52.

Add yellow through the mid-strip. The original's mean G stays above 100 out to about pixel 26 and above 20 out to pixel 38; the port drops below 100 by pixel 9 and below 20 by pixel 27. The result is that the port reads as a red fire with a small yellow tip while the original reads as a yellow-cored fire with red edges. Mean G over the strip should roughly double (37 -> 86) without moving mean R much (120 -> 186).
Make the base hotter/whiter: the original's first few pixels average B ~110-140 in its hot regime versus the port's ~40-50, i.e. noticeably more white-hot flicker at the fire root.

Soften and thicken the ember texture. The original's rightward trails are broad overlapping slabs; the port's are thin, sparse, high-contrast streaks with a lot of black between them. Wider/longer-lived heat cells (or more inter-pixel diffusion) would close this.

Speed: the port advects at a constant ~56 px/s at every frame rate while the original moves ~1.7-2 px per FRAME (33 px/s at our default 20 fps). Slowing the port to ~33 px/s would match at 20 fps, but note the original's speed is frame-coupled on our engine, so the honest fix is a per-second speed the fixer is willing to defend rather than a match at one rate — flag it as needing a hardware check.
Do not try to reproduce the original's ~33 s dead-freeze stretches; those are an engine clock artefact, and the port's uninterrupted animation is the correct behaviour.
